newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Michael Collins film stirs controversy [CORRECTED 22:39 GMT].
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Michael Collins film stirs controversy [CORRECTED 22:39 GMT].

text.p: When the film "Michael Collins" premiered last month at the Venice Film Festival, the audience responded with a 10-minute standing ovation.

At Toronto's film festival a week later, Neil Jordan's $28 million drama about the Irishman who created modern guerrilla warfare with the IRA in the 1920s, sparked a disturbance at one screening as one man started shouting "Death to the British", leading to a noisy debate in the audience.
(Corrects by deleting phrase "nearly sparked a riot" and makes clear that only one man shouted).
"Collins" has been fuelling controversy since it went into production last year in Dublin.

Although it won the top prize in Venice, the Golden Lion for Best Film, as well as a Best Actor award for "Schindler's List" star Liam Neeson, who plays the martyred Collins, the movie is not a glorification of guerrilla warfare, said Jordan, its writer-director.
The film opens in the United States this week and is expected to play in Britain before the end of the year.

"I make no apology, 'Yesterday's terrorist is today's statesman,'" states Jordan, citing independence struggles in Israel and Vietnam. "To me the film shows the attempt of one character who was engaged in warfare and who tried to replace warfare with politics, and that is the continuing story of the relationship between Ireland and Britain, definitely. I don't have to justify that."

As the filmmaker behind "The Crying Game" about a British soldier in Ireland caught up in IRA violence, Jordan well knows any telling of this part of Irish history is bound to arouse intense feelings.

"There has been a huge amount of comment about this movie in the British and Irish press before anyone had seen the movie or read the script or knew anything about it," he said. "Those people who have been making adverse commentary about the movie, who have since seen the film, have totally changed their opinion."

Despite instances of historical compression and dramatic license, Jordan said "Michael Collins," which features Julia Roberts in a small role, is "as accurate as a historical movie can be. I would challenge anybody to tell me a picture that is more historically accurate than this film."

Collins died in an ambush in 1922 as a partitioned Ireland became a reality because of a treaty he had signed with the British. Ratification of that treaty led to Collins' split with Eamon de Valera, the American-born Irish-Catholic revolutionary who would later serve as Ireland's president for generations.

In Jordan's movie de Valera is played by veteran British actor Alan Rickman, best known as the villain in "Die Hard." The film suggests that de Valera had a hand in Collins' death -- comparable, for the Irish, to Oliver Stone suggesting that Richard Nixon had a hand in John F. Kennedy's assassination.
"I do not say that Eamon de Valera arranged to have Michael Collins killed," Jordan countered even as he conceded, "There is a suggestion of it."
He noted, "The only thing I've said in the movie is Michael Collins is shot on his way while attempting a meeting with Eamon de Valera -- and that is true."

The film is obviously no "JFK" because Kennedy's sister, U.S. Ambassador to Ireland Jean Kennedy Smith, makes a cameo appearance in the film as a woman surprised to see the escaping Collins drop from a skylight into her hallway.
Still, there are some who see the anti-British warfare as another fund-raising tool among Americans for the IRA. With the passion that "Collins" has generated, should the film be banned in Britain?
"I think it's a very moving and very traumatic film. When the British and Irish public can see this film, I think that should be," Jordan said.

"As for whether things have changed between Britain and Ireland, one of the interesting things about the film is it will prompt people to ask that question: Have things changed? Maybe that's one of the reasons the film is worthy of debate."
